newsitem.title: USA: Ohio college paper gets access to crime records.
newsitem.headline: Ohio college paper gets access to crime records.

text.p: An Ohio college newspaper gained a far-reaching victory for freedom of the press when the Ohio Supreme Court ruled students should have access to student disciplinary records, the students' attorney said Thursday. By a 5-2 majority, the court Wednesday upheld the newspaper's right to obtain and publish information about offenses on the Miami University campus, using student disciplinary records that the university had withheld under federal privacy laws.

Marc Mezibov, a Cincinnati attorney representing the campus newspaper The Miami Student, said the ruling could extend beyond the current case. Miami University is a state-affiliated liberal arts college in Oxford, Ohio.
"While this decision is not binding on other states, it is a very important precedent where conflicts arise on this issue in other jurisdictions," he said.

The newspaper did not seek the names of students charged with wrongdoing but asked for disclosure of their ages and genders, the general location and nature of the incidents and the penalties imposed.
Jennifer Markiewicz, 22, editor when the newspaper first asked for the information, said she wanted to build a database for tracking student crime and punishment.

Markiewicz, who has graduated from Miami and plans to enter law school, said she could not understand why such records could be kept confidential on campus when similar information was accessible to the public in court records.

A spokesman for Miami University said it would comply by releasing the records. Richard Little, senior director of university communications, said the court decision would provide needed guidance in balancing federal privacy restrictions and Ohio's open-records law.
